newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel TV says police recommend charging Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Israel TV says police recommend charging Netanyahu.

text.p: Israel's Channel One television said on Wednesday that police had recommended charging Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a corruption case that has threatened his government.
It said police had recommended in a 995-page report to the state prosecution on Tuesday that he be charged with fraud and breach of trust in the appointment of an attorney general.
"So far as I know it's not correct and in any event the one to decide on submission of indictments is the prosecution and not the police," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak told the television.

Channel One quoted opposition leader Shimon Peres as saying that were the report true, it would be "a political earthquake" and warrant calling early elections. Netanyahu ousted Peres in elections only 11 months ago.
Israeli media had said police were recommending indicting three figures close to Netanyahu. But the television said it had learned that police had also recommended charging Netanyahu.
Prosecutors, who must decide whether to bring charges, had asked that the police report be kept under wraps for a few days while they considered whether to bring charges.
But with the disclosure on Channel One -- and a similar report on rival Channel Two -- prosecutors ordered police to immediately release the report, the channels said.
Police have been looking into Netanyahu's ill-fated appointment of lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney general since January.
At the time Channel One alleged that a Netanyahu ally on trial, politician Aryeh Deri, had pushed Roni Bar-On for the job in hopes of winning a plea bargain.
Bar-On himself quit hours after being appointed amid criticism he was professionally unfit for the job. The case has dominated the Israeli press during the 12 weeks of police investigation,
Bazak, Netanyahu's spokesman, suggested someone was trying to influence the prosecutors to bring charges.

"These leaks from the conclusions of the police at every stage in recent months, even this evening if it's at all true, raise a suspicion that perhaps they or someone there intends to influence the recommendations of the prosecution," he said.
"In any event I have no doubt, no doubt whatsoever, that the prime minister has no problem with this affair -- that he will emerge completely clean from this matter," he said.
"So far as it touches on the prime minister, this affair is complete nonsense. No such thing ever happened."
